etymology: Acronym for joy of missing out, coined as the answer to FOMO (fear of missing out, which Patrick McGinnis put in print in the Harbus at Harvard Business School in 2004). The tech writer Anil Dash is credited with the first public use in a July 2012 blog post titled "JOMO!", written after the birth of his son kept him off the party circuit and he found he did not mind. Christina Crook’s book The Joy of Missing Out (2015) carried it into the self-help aisle, and by the late 2010s it was a wellness hashtag for the phone-down, stay-home evening.
biblical_def: JOMO is the Millennial name for the relief of opting out: the evening you skip the event, silence the group chat, leave the feed unread, and discover you are glad you did. It began as a correction to FOMO, the anxious hunger to be wherever the photos are being taken, and it says something true. The heart was not made to be everywhere at once, and the craving to be is a symptom of a soul that has not found its rest. The Christian observation: JOMO is half a truth looking for its other half. Missing out is not itself the joy; it only clears the room for one. "In thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore" (Psa 16:11). The man who has that does not need every invitation, because he is not starving. Paul had "learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content" (Php 4:11), and the Preacher priced the trade exactly: "Better is an handful with quietness, than both the hands full with travail and vexation of spirit" (Ecc 4:6). Even the Lord drew His tired disciples away from the crowd: "Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while" (Mar 6:31). A father tells his son: you will be invited to more than you can attend, and most of it will not matter in a month; learn to say no without guilt and yes to the few things that are yours. He tells his daughter: the quiet evening is not a loss if you spend it with the Lord, your people, and a clean conscience.
webster_summary: Millennial slang (2012, Anil Dash; mainstream later 2010s) for the contentment of skipping the event and the feed; FOMO’s cure, redeemable when the room it clears is filled with the fulness of joy in God’s presence (Psa 16:11).
webster_full: JOMO, n. (Millennial slang, 2012–present; acronym of joy of missing out) The contentment of staying out of an event, a trend, or the feed and finding one does not regret it. "Cancelled plans, sweatpants, a book. Full JOMO."
Coined as the antonym of FOMO; often paired with "digital detox," "phone-free evening," and "protecting my peace."

Webster (1828), root joy: JOY, noun 1. The passion or emotion excited by the acquisition or expectation of good; that excitement of pleasurable feelings which is caused by success, good fortune, the gratification of desire or some good possessed, or by a rational prospect of possessing what we love or desire; gladness; exultation; exhilaration of spirits. JOY is a delight of the mind, from the consideration of the present or assured approaching possession of a good. […]
Decode for parents: a child who reaches for JOMO is reaching for rest; help him fill the cleared evening with something better than a second screen.
scriptures: Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore.
Php 4:11
Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.
Ecc 4:6
Better is an handful with quietness, than both the hands full with travail and vexation of spirit.
Mar 6:31
And he said unto them, Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while: for there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.
Heb 13:5
Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.
corruption_summary: JOMO can be contentment, or it can be a pleasant name for withdrawal; Scripture blesses the quiet hand that rests in God and rebukes the one that only retreats into self.
corruption_paragraphs: The word’s danger is that it can bless the wrong retreat. "Missing out" on a drunken party is wisdom; missing out on the church, the sick friend, and the family table because staying in is easier is not joy but sloth wearing a cosy sweater. Solomon warned that "Through desire a man, having separated himself, seeketh and intermeddleth with all wisdom" (Pro 18:1), and the author of Hebrews told the church not to be "forsaking the assembling of ourselves together" (Heb 10:25). JOMO practised as self-protection from every claim on our time turns a remedy into a fortress, and a fortress of one is a lonely place to keep house.

The redemption is to ask what the cleared evening is for. The Sabbath is the original joy of missing out: one day in seven when Israel missed the market on purpose and was the richer for it. Christian contentment is not indifference; it is satisfaction in a Giver. "Be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee" (Heb 13:5). Teach the young that the opposite of FOMO is not merely staying home; it is being so filled with the presence of God that the world’s invitations lose their pull, and the real invitations, to love and serve, become easy to accept.
roots_summary: Joy + of missing out: the 2012 inversion of FOMO (2004) → 2015 self-help title → late-2010s wellness hashtag for the phone-down evening.
roots_lines: Middle English joie, from Old French, Latin gaudium — gladness, delight
2004: FOMO printed by Patrick McGinnis (Harvard Business School Harbus)
July 2012: Anil Dash, blog post "JOMO!" — the first public antonym
2015: Christina Crook, The Joy of Missing Out; late 2010s: wellness and digital-detox hashtag
Biblical anchor: fulness of joy in God’s presence (Psa 16:11); content with such things as ye have (Heb 13:5)
usage: "Skipped the concert, read on the porch, slept nine hours. Peak JOMO."
JOMO clears the evening; only the presence of God fills it (Psa 16:11).
Better is an handful with quietness than two hands full of vexation (Ecc 4:6).

etymology: An old word with three lives. The verb swag (to sway, to sag under its own weight) is Middle English, likely Scandinavian; Shakespeare’s Puck sneers at "hempen home-spuns … swaggering here" (A Midsummer Night’s Dream, c. 1595), and swagger has meant a strutting gait ever since. Eighteenth-century thieves’ cant made swag the loot in the bag. The Millennial sense, shortened from swagger, came out of 1990s–2000s hip-hop: style, cool confidence, effortless presence. Soulja Boy’s "Turn My Swag On" (2008) and Justin Bieber’s ubiquity made it the word of 2010–2012, until "#swag" became an ironic joke. Separately, conference swag means free branded merchandise.
biblical_def: Swag is the Millennial word for a visible, unbothered confidence: the walk, the clothes, the way a person carries himself as if the room were his. To have swag is to look like you belong and to know it; to "turn your swag on" is to switch the self-assurance up for an audience. The Christian observation: confidence is not a sin, and timidity is no virtue. "The righteous are bold as a lion" (Pro 28:1). But Scripture always asks where confidence is planted. Swag is confidence rooted in the self and displayed to the crowd; its old cousin swagger names the gait of pride exactly. God’s answer is a different ground for the same boldness: "Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches: But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me" (Jer 9:23-24). The man who glories in the Lord can walk into any room without needing it to notice him. "Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth" (Pro 27:2). A father tells his son: carry yourself like a man who fears God and therefore fears nobody else; that is a confidence no outfit can give and no crowd can take. He tells his daughter: the boy with swag and no Lord is all walk and no ground.
webster_summary: Millennial slang (2000s hip-hop → 2010–12 peak) for a visible, cool self-confidence and style; boldness rooted in self and shown to a crowd, which Scripture re-roots in glorying in the Lord (Jer 9:24).
webster_full: SWAG, n. (Millennial slang, 2000s–2010s; clipped from swagger) Cool, stylish self-assurance; a visible confidence in how one dresses, walks, and speaks. "He’s got swag." Also swaggy, swagged out, "turn my swag on."
By 2012 used ironically ("#swag," "#YOLO #swag"); separately, swag = free branded merchandise at an event.
Webster (1828), root swag: SWAG, verb intransitive To sink down by its weight; to lean.
Decode for parents: swag is the confidence of being looked at; teach the confidence of being known by God.
scriptures: Pro 28:1
The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion.

Thus saith the LORD, Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches: But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the LORD which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, saith the LORD.
Pro 27:2
Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth; a stranger, and not thine own lips.
Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
Likewise, ye younger, submit yourselves unto the elder. Yea, all of you be subject one to another, and be clothed with humility: for God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble.
corruption_summary: Swag makes confidence a performance rooted in self; Scripture keeps the boldness and moves its ground: let him that glorieth glory in the Lord.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption in swag is not the confidence but the root and the audience. It is self-assurance that depends on being seen, and so it must always be maintained, refreshed, and displayed. That is why the word’s older form, swagger, has always meant the strut of a proud man. Scripture’s verdict on that posture is blunt: "Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall" (Pro 16:18). The swaggering self is also fragile; the moment the room stops watching, the confidence drains away, because it was never anchored in anything but the room.

The biblical recovery keeps the boldness and replaces the ground. Peter and John, "unlearned and ignorant men," stood before the council with such boldness that the rulers "took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus" (Act 4:13). That is swag redeemed: a confidence that comes from company with Christ rather than from clothes or crowd. "God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble" (1Pe 5:5). Teach the young to stand straight, speak clearly, and look a man in the eye, not because they are impressive but because they belong to Someone who is.
roots_summary: Middle English swag (to sway) → swagger (Shakespeare, c. 1595) → thieves’ cant swag (loot) → 2000s hip-hop swag (cool confidence) → 2012 ironic hashtag.
roots_lines: Middle English swaggen, probably Scandinavian (Norwegian svagga, to sway) — to sag, to sway
c. 1595: swaggering in Shakespeare — a strutting, blustering gait
18th c. thieves’ cant: swag — plunder, the bag of loot
1990s–2000s hip-hop: swag clipped from swagger — style and self-assurance; 2008 "Turn My Swag On"
Biblical anchor: the righteous are bold as a lion (Pro 28:1); glory in knowing the Lord (Jer 9:24)
usage: "New kicks, fresh cut, he walked in with mad swag."
Swag needs a room to notice; godly boldness only needs to have been with Jesus (Act 4:13).
Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth (Pro 27:2).

etymology: From Greek epikos, from epos (word, song), through Latin epicus; in English since the 1580s for the long heroic poem (Homer, Virgil, Milton’s Paradise Lost). The Millennial sense grew on the early-2000s internet and in gaming, where epic tiers of loot (World of Warcraft, 2004, colour-coded epic gear purple) and "epic win" / "epic fail" spread the adjective to anything large, impressive, or memorable: an epic party, an epic sandwich, an epic road trip. By about 2008 it was the default Millennial superlative, and by 2012 it was mocked as overused.
biblical_def: Epic in Millennial speech means enormous, legendary, unforgettable: anything that feels bigger than ordinary life. The word borrows the dignity of the old heroic poem and spends it on a burrito. The Christian observation: the word is harmless in itself, and the hunger beneath it is holy. Men want to live inside a great story, and they are right to want it, because they do. The true epic is the history of redemption, from the garden to the city, told by the God who is "Declaring the end from the beginning" (Isa 46:10). Scripture’s own account of the faithful runs out of time before it runs out of heroes: "the time would fail me to tell of Gedeon, and of Barak, and of Samson, and of Jephthae" (Heb 11:32). John ends his Gospel by saying that if everything Jesus did were written, "the world itself could not contain the books that should be written" (Joh 21:25). That is the scale the word was made for. The danger is only inflation: when every lunch is epic, nothing is, and the vocabulary for wonder is worn out before a young man meets the things that deserve it. A father tells his son: save your biggest words for the biggest things, and you will still have them when you stand at a graveside, a wedding, or the empty tomb. Teach the children that their small lives are written into the one story that is really epic.
webster_summary: Millennial slang (2000s internet and gaming) for anything huge, impressive, or legendary; a harmless inflation of the heroic-poem word, whose true object is the history of redemption (Isa 46:10).
webster_full: EPIC, adj. / n. (Millennial slang, 2000s–2010s) Impressive, enormous, legendary; also as an exclamation: "Epic!" Phrases: epic win, epic fail, epic fail compilations; epic loot tier in online gaming.

Webster (1828), root epic: EPIC, adjective [Latin epicus; Gr. a song, or to speak.] Narrative; containing narration; rehearsing. An epic poem, otherwise called heroic, is a poem which narrates a story, real or fictitious or both, representing, in an elevated style, some signal action or series of actions and events, usually the achievements of some distinguished hero, and intended to form the morals and affect the mind with the love of virtue. […]
Decode for parents: the word is a craving for a great story; give your children the one they are actually in.
scriptures: Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure:
And what shall I more say? for the time would fail me to tell of Gedeon, and of Barak, and of Samson, and of Jephthae; of David also, and Samuel, and of the prophets:
And there are also many other things which Jesus did, the which, if they should be written every one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written. Amen.
One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts.
But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.
corruption_summary: Epic spends the dignity of the heroic poem on lunch; harmless, but it wears out the words for wonder before the young meet the true epic of redemption.
corruption_paragraphs: The quiet loss in epic is linguistic. When the superlative becomes the everyday adjective, the language of awe is debased, and Scripture takes our words seriously: "every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment" (Mat 12:36). That is not a ban on enthusiasm; it is a call to proportion. A generation that called a pizza epic will need other words for the resurrection, and often finds it has none left, so the mighty acts of God sound no larger than a playlist.

The redemption is to restore the word to its object. The Psalmist hands the epic down the generations: "One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts" (Psa 145:4). Read the young the long story: creation, fall, flood, exodus, kingdom, exile, the cross, the empty tomb, the coming King. Then the word epic has something to point to, and a teenager who loves great stories discovers that he was born into the greatest one, with a part to play in it.
roots_summary: Greek epos (word, song) → epikos → Latin epicus → English epic (1580s, heroic poem) → 2000s internet / gaming superlative.
roots_lines: Greek epos — word, song; epikos — pertaining to heroic song
1580s English: epic — the long narrative poem of heroes (Homer, Virgil, Milton)
2004: World of Warcraft’s purple epic loot tier; gaming spreads the adjective
c. 2005–2012: epic, epic win, epic fail as the default Millennial superlative
Biblical anchor: declaring the end from the beginning (Isa 46:10); the world could not contain the books (Joh 21:25)
usage: "That road trip was epic, bro."
Call the sandwich good; save epic for the empty tomb.
One generation shall declare God’s mighty acts to another (Psa 145:4).

etymology: The noun-interjection fail traces to the broken English of a 1998 Japanese arcade game, Blazing Star, whose game-over screen read "You fail it! Your skill is not enough." Imageboards around 2003 seized it, and "FAIL" stamped over a photo became a meme. Epic fail followed by about 2005, and in 2008 the humour site FAIL Blog (later part of Cheezburger) turned it into an industry of captioned disasters: the misspelled tattoo, the truck wedged under the bridge, the skateboarder meeting the railing. It was a Millennial staple through the early 2010s, now largely displaced by video compilations.
biblical_def: An epic fail is a spectacular, public, usually funny failure, captured and shared: the botched backflip, the wedding cake on the floor, the sign that says the opposite of what it meant. The phrase is also turned on oneself ("epic fail on my part") as a light way to own a mistake. The Christian observation has two edges. First, there is a grace in being able to laugh at our own blunders; pride cannot do it, and humility can. Second, there is no grace in a culture that harvests other people’s humiliation for entertainment. "Whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker: and he that is glad at calamities shall not be unpunished" (Pro 17:5). "Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth" (Pro 24:17); if not over an enemy, how much less over a stranger whose worst moment went viral. And the gospel speaks a stranger word over failure itself: "For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again" (Pro 24:16). The Church is full of epic fails: Peter’s denial, Jonah’s flight, David’s rooftop. Their stories are told not as comedy but as mercy, because the Lord restores. A father tells his son: when you fail in front of everyone, own it, laugh if it is funny, and get up; and never make another man’s fall your entertainment.
webster_summary: Millennial slang (from a 1998 game’s "You fail it," 2003 meme, 2008 FAIL Blog) for a spectacular public failure; fine as self-mockery, wrong as entertainment harvested from another’s humiliation (Pro 17:5).
webster_full: EPIC FAIL, n. / interj. (Millennial slang, c. 2005–2015) A spectacular, usually public and comic failure; also said as a verdict: "Epic fail." Short form: fail ("FAIL," "#fail").
Genre: FAIL Blog (2008), fail compilations, captioned photos of botched signs, stunts, and repairs.

Webster (1828), root fail: FAIL, verb intransitive [Latin fallo; Gr. whence; Eng. felony. It seems to be allied to fall, fallow, pale, and many other words.] 1. To become deficient; to be insufficient; to cease to be abundant for supply; or to be entirely wanting. We say, in a dry season, the springs and streams fail or are failing, before they are entirely exhausted. We say also, the springs failed, when they entirely ceased to flow. Crops fail wholly or partially. 2. To decay; to decline; to sink; to be diminished. […]
Decode for parents: the joke trains children to laugh at strangers’ worst moments; teach them to laugh at their own and to help others up.
scriptures: Pro 17:5
Whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker: and he that is glad at calamities shall not be unpunished.
Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth:
For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again: but the wicked shall fall into mischief.
Mic 7:8
Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me.
Gal 6:1
Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.
corruption_summary: Epic fail turns another person’s humiliation into content; Scripture forbids gladness at calamity and answers failure with restoration.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the spectator’s seat. The FAIL genre runs on strangers who never consented to be laughed at by millions, and it trains the viewer to meet a fall with a smirk instead of a hand. Scripture calls that posture dangerous to the one who holds it: he that is glad at calamities "shall not be unpunished" (Pro 17:5). The mocker also forgets his own turn is coming; the man who laughs loudest at the fail video has his own recorded on some phone he never noticed.

The biblical recovery is a theology of getting up. "Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me" (Mic 7:8). Failure is not the end of a believer’s story, and the brother who sees it has a job: "if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted" (Gal 6:1). Raise children who can laugh at their own spilled milk, who refuse to forward a stranger’s humiliation, and who know that the Lord who restored Peter on the shore restores His people still.
roots_summary: Blazing Star (1998) "You fail it!" → 2003 imageboard "FAIL" → c. 2005 epic fail → 2008 FAIL Blog → 2010s fail-compilation videos.
roots_lines: Latin fallere — to deceive, to disappoint; Old French faillir — to be lacking
1998: arcade game Blazing Star — "You fail it! Your skill is not enough"
c. 2003: imageboard FAIL meme; c. 2005: epic fail
2008: FAIL Blog launches; 2010s: fail-compilation videos on YouTube
Biblical anchor: a just man falleth seven times and riseth up again (Pro 24:16); restore such an one (Gal 6:1)
usage: "He tried to jump the creek and landed in it. Epic fail."
Laugh at your own epic fail; never make another man’s fall your entertainment (Pro 24:17).
When I fall, I shall arise (Mic 7:8).

etymology: A deliberate misspelling of owned (soundly beaten, dominated), from early-2000s online gaming. The p sits beside the o on a QWERTY keyboard, and a much-repeated (unverified) legend credits a Warcraft map-maker’s typo, "has been pwned," for the form. Hacker and gamer culture kept the typo on purpose as an in-group mark; pwnage and pwn followed. In 2013 the security researcher Troy Hunt launched the data-breach checker Have I Been Pwned, which gave the word a second, more sober life: to be pwned is to have your accounts compromised.
biblical_def: To be pwned is to be utterly beaten, outplayed, humiliated in a game or argument; to have pwned someone is to have dominated him so thoroughly that the victory is a public mockery. In security talk it means your data has been taken. The Christian observation starts with the root word the typo hides: owned. Every person is owned by something. The gamer’s boast is that he owns his opponent; the gospel’s claim is that none of us owns himself. "What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price" (1Co 6:19-20). There is a real defeat in Scripture that dwarfs every match: at the cross Christ, "having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it" (Col 2:15). That is the only pwnage worth celebrating, and the victory belongs to Him. In ordinary contests, Scripture asks for a victor’s humility: "Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth" (Pro 24:17). A father tells his son: win hard, lose well, and never rub a beaten man’s face in it; a gracious winner is rarer than a skilled one. And remember whose you are before you boast about whom you have beaten.
webster_summary: Millennial gamer slang (early 2000s typo of owned) for being utterly beaten or, since 2013, hacked; its hidden root asks who owns us: ye are not your own, ye are bought with a price (1Co 6:20).
webster_full: PWNED, v. (Millennial gamer slang, early 2000s; typo-spelling of owned) Utterly defeated, dominated, humiliated. "You just got pwned." Also pwn, pwnage.
Security sense (2013–present, Have I Been Pwned): having one’s accounts or data compromised in a breach.

Webster (1828), root own: OWN, adjective [ See Owe and Ought .] 1. Belonging to; possessed; peculiar; usually expressing property with emphasis, or in express exclusion of others. It follows my, your, his, their, thy, her. God created man in his own image. Adam begat a son in his own likeness. Let them fall by their own counsel. He washed us from our sins in his own blood. In the phrases, his own nations, his own country, the word own denotes that the person belongs to the nation or country. 2. own often follows a verb; […]
Decode for parents: the word is trash talk; the root is a catechism question — whose are you?
scriptures: What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's.
Col 2:15
And having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it.
Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth:
Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.
For whatsoever is born of God overcometh the world: and this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith.
corruption_summary: Pwned celebrates domination and humiliation of the beaten; Scripture forbids gloating and points to the one decisive triumph, Christ’s over the powers.
corruption_paragraphs: The word carries the culture of trash talk: victory is not complete until the loser is mocked. Online, where opponents are faceless, that cruelty comes cheap, and boys learn to measure themselves by how thoroughly they can humiliate someone else. Scripture refuses the posture even toward real enemies: "Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth" (Pro 24:17). The gloater is not strong; he is still hungry, needing the other man’s shame to feel his own win.

The recovery is to know the real war and the real Victor. "Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good" (Rom 12:21). The Christian does fight, but his weapons are faith and goodness, and his victory is borrowed: "whatsoever is born of God overcometh the world: and this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith" (1Jn 5:4). Let the young compete with fire and lose with grace, and teach them that the most important sentence about ownership was written in blood: ye are bought with a price.
roots_summary: Old English agen (own) → gamer owned (defeated) → typo pwned (early 2000s) → 2013 security sense (data breached).
roots_lines: Old English agnian — to possess, to make one’s own
1990s gamer slang: owned — decisively beaten
Early 2000s: keyboard-slip pwned kept on purpose; pwn, pwnage
2013: Troy Hunt’s Have I Been Pwned — the breach sense
Biblical anchor: ye are not your own (1Co 6:19); Christ triumphing over the powers (Col 2:15)
usage: "Three headshots in ten seconds. Pwned."
You were pwned at a game; you were purchased at a price (1Co 6:20).
Overcome evil with good, not with trash talk (Rom 12:21).

etymology: From newbie, itself attested in Usenet and US military slang of the 1980s (likely from new boy or Australian newie). Online gamers of the late 1990s and 2000s clipped it to newb and then noob (also written n00b), and an informal distinction grew up: a newb is simply new and willing to learn; a noob is incompetent and will not. By the mid-2000s it was general Millennial slang for any beginner or bumbler ("noob mistake").
biblical_def: A noob is a beginner, and in gamer usage usually a contemptible one: the player who does not know the map, wastes ammunition, and gets the team killed. To call someone a noob is to mark him as beneath the group. The Christian observation: every one of us was a noob, and the Church is a school for beginners. The Lord did not despise new things: "For who hath despised the day of small things?" (Zec 4:10). Paul told a young pastor, "Let no man despise thy youth" (1Ti 4:12), and the Lord Jesus warned, "Take heed that ye despise not one of these little ones" (Mat 18:10). Scripture does expect growth; it scolds believers who stay infants when they should be teachers, for "every one that useth milk is unskilful in the word of righteousness: for he is a babe" (Heb 5:13). So the biblical word has both halves of the gamer distinction: the newborn is honoured, the one who refuses to grow is rebuked. "As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby" (1Pe 2:2). A father tells his son: the veteran who mocks beginners has forgotten who taught him; be the one who shows the new man where to stand. And be teachable yourself, because the only shameful kind of noob is the one who will not learn.
webster_summary: Millennial gamer slang (late 1990s–2000s, from newbie) for a beginner, usually a contemptible one; Scripture honours the newborn, despises not the day of small things (Zec 4:10), and rebukes only the refusal to grow.
webster_full: NOOB, n. (Millennial gamer slang, late 1990s–2000s; also n00b, newb) A beginner; especially an unskilled player who will not learn. "Noob mistake."
In-group distinction: newb = new and teachable; noob = incompetent and proud of it.

Webster (1828), root new: NEW, adjective 1. Lately made, invented, produced or come into being; that has existed a short time only; recent in origin; novel; opposed to old, and used of things; as a new coat; a new house; a new book; a new fashion; a new theory; the new chimistry; a new discovery. 2. Lately introduced to our knowledge; not before known; recently discovered; as a new metal; a new species of animals or plants found in foreign countries; the new continent. 3. Modern; not ancient. 4. Recently produced by change; as a new life. […]
Decode for parents: ask your child how his group treats the new kid; the answer tells you what kind of team it is.
scriptures: Zec 4:10

For who hath despised the day of small things? for they shall rejoice, and shall see the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel with those seven; they are the eyes of the LORD, which run to and fro through the whole earth.
Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.
Take heed that ye despise not one of these little ones; for I say unto you, That in heaven their angels do always behold the face of my Father which is in heaven.
Heb 5:13
For every one that useth milk is unskilful in the word of righteousness: for he is a babe.
As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby:
corruption_summary: Noob makes beginners objects of contempt; Scripture honours the newborn and the day of small things, and rebukes only the refusal to grow.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is a hierarchy built on skill, policed by mockery. The word lets the experienced player forget that everything he knows was taught to him, and it teaches the new player to hide his ignorance rather than ask. That is the opposite of the Church, where the strong are told to bear "the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves" (Rom 15:1), and the mature are expected to turn and teach.

The redemption honours both halves of the old gamer distinction. The beginner is to be welcomed, fed, and patiently trained; the believer who refuses to grow is to be lovingly rebuked. Apollos was mighty in the Scriptures and still a learner when Aquila and Priscilla "took him unto them, and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly" (Act 18:26). That is the model: no contempt for the new man, no excuse for staying new. Let the young be humble enough to be noobs and generous enough to train them.
roots_lines: Old English niwe — new, fresh, recent
1970s–80s: newbie in military and Usenet slang
Late 1990s gaming: newb, noob, n00b (leetspeak spelling)
2000s: noob generalized to any bumbler; "noob mistake"
Biblical anchor: despise not the day of small things (Zec 4:10); as newborn babes desire the milk (1Pe 2:2)
usage: "Don’t be a noob, cover the left side."
Every veteran was a noob once; teach the new man (Act 18:26).
Despise not the day of small things (Zec 4:10).

etymology: Clipped from elite. In 1980s bulletin-board culture, "elite" boards granted members access to pirated software and restricted files; insiders wrote the word in a code that swapped letters for look-alike numbers and symbols: 31337 (eleet), 1337 (leet). The cipher, leetspeak, spread through hacker groups such as the Cult of the Dead Cow and into 1990s–2000s online gaming ("l33t skillz," "n00b," "pwn"), where it marked skill and insider status. By the late 2000s it survived mostly as a self-mocking Millennial joke.
biblical_def: Leet means elite: highly skilled, in the know, part of the inner circle, especially in gaming and hacking. Leetspeak is the code (1337, h4x0r, pwn3d) that once kept outsiders out. The Christian observation: the word is a small picture of an old temptation, the pride of secret knowledge. The early Church fought a whole movement built on it, the gnostic boast of an enlightened few with a hidden code. Scripture answers that the knowledge which matters was spoken in the open. Jesus told the high priest, "I spake openly to the world; I ever taught in the synagogue, and in the temple … and in secret have I said nothing" (Joh 18:20). The gospel is not a password but a proclamation, and God has chosen to hide it from the self-appointed elite: "thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes" (Mat 11:25). Skill is a gift and may be honoured, and Scripture admires the man "diligent in his business" who "shall stand before kings" (Pro 22:29). But "Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth" (1Co 8:1). A father tells his son: get good at things, really good, and then use the skill to serve rather than to sort people into insiders and noobs. The circle that matters has a door anyone may enter through Christ.
webster_summary: Millennial slang from 1980s hacker code (1337, from elite) for elite skill and insider status; skill may be honoured, but knowledge puffeth up, and the gospel is proclaimed openly, not passworded (1Co 8:1; Joh 18:20).
webster_full: LEET, adj. / n. (Millennial gamer and hacker slang; 1980s–2000s; written 1337) Elite; highly skilled; belonging to the in-group. "Leet skills." Leetspeak: the cipher substituting numerals and symbols for letters (h4x0r = hacker).
Now chiefly ironic or nostalgic; survives in usernames and as a programmer in-joke (port 31337).
No Webster 1828 entry for the root elite, a French word that entered general English use after Webster’s dictionary.
Decode for parents: watch for groups whose identity depends on a code that keeps others out; Christ’s people speak plainly.
scriptures: Jesus answered him, I spake openly to the world; I ever taught in the synagogue, and in the temple, whither the Jews always resort; and in secret have I said nothing.
At that time Jesus answered and said, I thank thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes.
Now as touching things offered unto idols, we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth.
Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men.
But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;
corruption_summary: Leet prizes exclusive skill and secret code; Scripture honours skill but rebukes the pride of hidden knowledge, because the gospel is proclaimed openly and revealed to babes.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is gnostic in miniature: worth measured by access to a code the crowd cannot read. Leetspeak was built to exclude, and the elite circle defined itself by who was kept out. That is the opposite of the Kingdom, where "God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise" (1Co 1:27), and the treasure is hidden not behind skill but behind humility, so that only those willing to become as little children find it.

The redemption honours real excellence without the velvet rope. The craftsman Bezaleel was filled "with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding" to build the tabernacle, and his skill served the worship of a whole people. Teach a gifted child to aim at mastery and to put it at the service of others, to explain rather than to gatekeep, and to remember that the greatest knowledge any of us has was given freely: "the entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple" (Psa 119:130).
roots_lines: Latin eligere — to pick out, to choose; French élite — the chosen part
1980s: "elite" bulletin boards with restricted files; the numeric cipher 31337
1990s: hacker groups and gaming adopt leetspeak (1337, h4x0r, n00b, pwn)
Late 2000s: survives as Millennial irony and programmer in-joke
Biblical anchor: in secret have I said nothing (Joh 18:20); knowledge puffeth up (1Co 8:1)
usage: "Dude, your speedrun was leet."
Get good, then teach; knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth (1Co 8:1).
The gospel has no password: in secret have I said nothing (Joh 18:20).

etymology: Acronym for laughing out loud (early on also lots of love, a sense that caused famous parental misunderstandings). Wayne Pearson has claimed coining it on the Viewline bulletin board in Calgary in the 1980s, and it circulated on Usenet by 1989. AOL chat rooms and AOL Instant Messenger (1997) made it universal; texting in the 2000s softened it from real laughter into a tone marker that means "I am being friendly" ("lol ok," "sorry lol"). The Oxford English Dictionary admitted it in 2011. Gen Z largely retired it for skull emojis and keyboard-smash.
biblical_def: LOL began as "laughing out loud" and became the Millennial generation’s punctuation: a lowercase lol at the end of a sentence now rarely means anyone laughed. It softens a request, cushions criticism, or covers embarrassment. The Christian observation: laughter itself is a gift of God, and the Bible is not embarrassed by it. There is "A time to weep, and a time to laugh" (Ecc 3:4); when the Lord turned again the captivity of Zion, "Then was our mouth filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing" (Psa 126:2); "A merry heart doeth good like a medicine" (Pro 17:22). A Christian home should ring with real laughter. But the reflexive lol is mostly not laughter; it is a mask. Scripture knew the mask too: "Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful; and the end of that mirth is heaviness" (Pro 14:13). The habit can blunt honesty ("just kidding lol"), take the edge off a cruelty, or hide real pain behind three letters. A father reads his teenager’s texts not for the jokes but for the lol at the end of something sad, and asks about it. He teaches his children to laugh with their whole hearts at what is truly funny, and to say plainly what they mean when it is not.
webster_summary: Millennial acronym (1980s BBS / Usenet; AIM and texting 2000s) for laughing out loud, worn down into a tone-softener; laughter is a gift (Ecc 3:4), but the reflexive lol can mask sorrow or cruelty (Pro 14:13).
webster_full: LOL, interj. (Millennial chat and text slang, 1980s–2010s; acronym of laughing out loud) Expressing amusement; by the 2000s chiefly a softener or tone marker. "lol ok." Variants: lolz, lulz (mischievous amusement), LOLing.
Admitted to the Oxford English Dictionary 2011; spoken aloud as "lawl."

Webster (1828), root laugh: LAUGH, verb intransitive l’aff. [Heb.] 1. To make the noise and exhibit the features which are characteristic of mirth in the human species. Violent laughter is accompanied with a shaking of the sides, and all laughter expels breath from the lungs. 2. In poetry, to be gay; to appear gay, cheerful, pleasant, lively or brilliant. Then laughs the childish year with flow’rets crown’d. And o’er the foaming bowl, the laughing wine. To laugh at, to ridicule; to treat with some degree of contempt. […]
Decode for parents: look for the lol after something sad; it is often a hand raised for help.
scriptures: Ecc 3:4
A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
Then was our mouth filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing: then said they among the heathen, The LORD hath done great things for them.
A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones.
Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful; and the end of that mirth is heaviness.
Eph 5:4
Neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient: but rather giving of thanks.
corruption_summary: LOL wore laughter down into a mask that softens, hides, and excuses; Scripture blesses real laughter and sees the sorrowful heart beneath false mirth.
corruption_paragraphs: The quiet corruption of lol is dishonesty by habit. It lets a hard word be said and disowned in the same breath, lets cruelty pass as banter, and lets a hurting child report something serious in a tone that asks no one to take it seriously. Paul names the vice of speech that is witty without being wholesome: "filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient: but rather giving of thanks" (Eph 5:4). Not all jesting is condemned there, but the jest that dodges truth and responsibility is.

The recovery is to restore laughter to its place and to recover plain speech. Real laughter, at a good story, at the baby’s first word, at our own folly, is a foretaste of the joy of the redeemed. The fake laughter of the reflexive acronym is a small lie told a thousand times a week. Teach the young to laugh out loud when something is funny, and to say "I’m hurting," "I’m sorry," or "I disagree" without three letters to hide behind.
roots_summary: Old English hlihhan (laugh) → 1980s BBS / Usenet acronym LOL → 1997 AIM → 2000s texting tone-marker → 2011 OED.
roots_lines: Old English hlihhan — to laugh
1980s: LOL on bulletin boards; 1989 on Usenet
1997–2000s: AIM, chat rooms, texting; meaning softens to a tone marker
2011: Oxford English Dictionary; lulz for mischievous fun
Biblical anchor: a time to laugh (Ecc 3:4); even in laughter the heart is sorrowful (Pro 14:13)
usage: "Missed the bus again lol."
A merry heart doeth good like a medicine (Pro 17:22); a habitual lol may be covering a wound.
Laugh out loud at what is funny; say plainly what is not.

etymology: Acronym for rolling on the floor laughing (also ROTFL), the escalation of LOL in early-1990s Usenet and IRC chat. Longer intensifiers followed (ROFLMAO), and the 2000s gamer joke roflcopter, an ASCII-art helicopter whose rotor spelled ROFL, made the acronym its own meme. Like LOL it was mostly typed, never done; by the 2010s Millennials used it ironically, and the rolling-on-the-floor-laughing emoji (Unicode 2016) took over the job.
biblical_def: ROFL claims a laugh so violent that one has fallen to the floor. Nobody has, of course; it is exaggeration as courtesy, the online way of telling a friend his joke landed. The Christian observation: the acronym is a small study in inflated speech. When every mild amusement must be reported as helpless hysteria, words lose their weight. The Lord Jesus asked for a simpler honesty: "let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil" (Mat 5:37). That is not a rule against humour; it is a call to let our words match the facts. Scripture also distinguishes kinds of laughter. There is the laughter God gives, as when Sarah said, "God hath made me to laugh, so that all that hear will laugh with me" (Gen 21:6). There is the noisy, empty laugh of the fool: "For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool" (Ecc 7:6). And there is the laughter that covers harm: "As a mad man who casteth firebrands, arrows, and death, So is the man that deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am not I in sport?" (Pro 26:18-19). A father teaches his children to enjoy a joke, to tell the truth about how funny it was, and never to use "just a joke" as a shield for wounding someone.
webster_summary: Millennial acronym (early 1990s, rolling on the floor laughing) inflating amusement into hysteria; harmless courtesy, but a lesson in inflated speech and in the laughter of the fool (Ecc 7:6; Mat 5:37).
webster_full: ROFL, interj. (Millennial chat slang, early 1990s–2010s; acronym of rolling on the floor laughing; also ROTFL) Expressing great amusement; typed, rarely meant. Intensified forms and memes: ROFLMAO, roflcopter.
Superseded in the late 2010s by the rolling-on-the-floor-laughing emoji.

Webster (1828), root roll: ROLL, verb transitive [It is usual to consider this word as formed by contraction from the Latin rotula, a little wheel, from rota.] 1. To move by turning on the surface, or with a circular motion in which all parts of the surface are successively applied to a plane; as, to roll a barrel or puncheon; to roll a stone or ball. Sisyphus was condemned to roll a stone to the top of a hill, which, when he had done so, rolled down again, and thus his punishment was eternal. 2. To revolve; to turn on its axis; […]
Decode for parents: exaggeration is the native tongue of the feed; teach children to make their words match the facts.
scriptures: Mat 5:37
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
Gen 21:6
And Sarah said, God hath made me to laugh, so that all that hear will laugh with me.
Ecc 7:6
For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool: this also is vanity.
As a mad man who casteth firebrands, arrows, and death, So is the man that deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am not I in sport?
Psa 2:4
He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh: the Lord shall have them in derision.
corruption_summary: ROFL makes exaggeration a courtesy and empties laughter of weight; Scripture asks for yea-yea honesty and distinguishes the laughter God gives from the crackling thorns of the fool.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is small and cumulative: speech inflated until it is worthless. A generation trained to report every chuckle as collapse finds it hard to say anything plainly, and the habit spreads from jokes to praise, outrage, and grief. The Preacher’s image fits the endless online laugh: thorns flaring loud under a pot and gone in a second, much noise, little heat. It also gives cover to the cruel joke, the "I was only kidding" that Proverbs compares to a madman throwing firebrands.

The recovery is the plain word and the true laugh. Scripture even records the laughter of God: "He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh" (Psa 2:4), not at a joke but at the folly of kings who rage against His Anointed. Holy laughter sees things as they are. Teach the young to laugh honestly, to praise honestly, and to let their yes be yes, so that when they do say something is the funniest thing they have ever heard, it will be believed.
roots_summary: Old French roller (roll) + laugh → early-1990s Usenet / IRC ROFL, ROTFL → ROFLMAO, roflcopter → 2016 emoji.
roots_lines: Latin rotula (little wheel) → Old French roller — to roll
Early 1990s: ROFL / ROTFL on Usenet and IRC
2000s: ROFLMAO; the roflcopter ASCII meme
2016: rolling-on-the-floor-laughing emoji replaces the acronym
Biblical anchor: let your communication be, Yea, yea (Mat 5:37); the crackling of thorns (Ecc 7:6)
usage: "ROFL that video of the goat on the trampoline."
Let your yea be yea, even about how funny it was (Mat 5:37).
"Am not I in sport?" is no excuse for a firebrand (Pro 26:19).

etymology: Initialism for Oh my God. Its first known written use is a 1917 letter from Admiral John Fisher to Winston Churchill ("O.M.G. (Oh! My God!)"), but the modern life began in 1990s chat rooms and exploded with 2000s texting. Millennials used it as a reflex for any surprise, delight, or outrage ("OMG I can’t," "OMG Becky"), and it moved from screens to speech, spoken as letters. The Oxford English Dictionary added it in 2011. Variants: OMFG (vulgar), OMGosh, omw is unrelated ("on my way").
biblical_def: OMG is "Oh my God" reduced to three letters and spent on everything: a sale, a celebrity, a cute dog, a bad grade. It is the most common use of the divine name in the Millennial vocabulary, and almost never a prayer. The Christian observation must be direct, because the commandment is: "Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain" (Exo 20:7). To take His name in vain is to lift it up emptily, to use it for no purpose, as filler or exclamation. The abbreviation does not change what is being said; it only makes it easier to say without noticing. The first petition of the Lord’s Prayer asks the opposite: "Hallowed be thy name" (Mat 6:9). "Holy and reverend is his name" (Psa 111:9). There is a right way to say these very words. When Thomas saw the risen Christ and touched His wounds, he said, "My Lord and my God" (Joh 20:28), and it was the truest confession in the Gospels. A father teaches his children both lessons at once: never spend God’s name on a pair of shoes, and always be ready to say it, with your whole heart, about Jesus Christ. Give them other words for surprise; there are hundreds.
webster_summary: Millennial initialism (1990s chat, 2000s texting; OED 2011) for Oh my God as a reflex exclamation; the divine name spent as filler, which the third commandment forbids (Exo 20:7). Reject.
webster_full: OMG, interj. (Millennial text and speech slang, 1990s–present; initialism of Oh my God) An exclamation of surprise, excitement, or dismay, applied to anything. Spoken as letters: "Oh-em-gee." Vulgar intensive: OMFG.
First recorded 1917 (Admiral Fisher to Churchill); mainstream with 2000s texting; Oxford English Dictionary 2011.

Webster (1828), root God: GOD, noun 1. The Supreme Being; Jehovah; the eternal and infinite spirit, the creator, and the sovereign of the universe. GOD is a spirit; and they that worship him, must worship him in spirit and in truth. John 4:24 . 2. A false god; a heathen deity; an idol. Fear not the gods of the Amorites. Judges 6:10 . 3. A prince; a ruler; a magistrate or judge; an angel. Thou shalt not revile the gods, nor curse the ruler of thy people. Exodus 22:28 . Psalms 97:7 . [Gods here is a bad translation.] 4. […]
Decode for parents: abbreviation does not change what is said; give your children other words for surprise and save the Name for worship.
scriptures: Exo 20:7
Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain.
Mat 6:9
After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name.
He sent redemption unto his people: he hath commanded his covenant for ever: holy and reverend is his name.
And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God.
Neither shall ye profane my holy name; but I will be hallowed among the children of Israel: I am the LORD which hallow you,
corruption_summary: OMG spends the name of God as filler for every surprise; the third commandment forbids taking His name in vain, and the abbreviation only makes the sin easier to miss.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the cheapening of the holiest word a mouth can say. Israel was commanded, "Neither shall ye profane my holy name; but I will be hallowed among the children of Israel" (Lev 22:32), and Jews of the Second Temple period feared misusing the Name so much that they stopped pronouncing it at all. Our culture has moved to the opposite pole: the Name is so constant in exclamation that it no longer registers as His. A child raised on OMG learns, without anyone teaching it, that God is a word one says when a cake looks good.

The recovery is not prudishness but reverence and readiness. The same three words are the summit of Christian confession on Thomas’s lips. Teach the young to guard the Name in casual speech and to hallow it in prayer; to substitute honest exclamations for the reflex; and, when they meet the risen Christ in His Word, to say "My Lord and my God" and mean every syllable. A tongue trained to reverence will not waste the Name, and will not be ashamed of it either.
roots_summary: "Oh my God" → 1917 O.M.G. (Fisher) → 1990s chat → 2000s texting reflex → spoken initialism → OED 2011.
roots_lines: Old English god — the Supreme Being; Hebrew Elohim, Greek theos
1917: "O.M.G. (Oh! My God!)" in Admiral Fisher’s letter to Churchill
1990s–2000s: chat and text initialism; spoken aloud by Millennials
2011: Oxford English Dictionary admits OMG
Biblical anchor: thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain (Exo 20:7); my Lord and my God (Joh 20:28)
usage: "OMG this latte is everything."
Hallowed be thy name (Mat 6:9): not spent on a latte.
The right use of the words: "My Lord and my God" (Joh 20:28).

etymology: Initialism for be right back, from 1980s–1990s IRC and AOL chat rooms, where typing it told the room you were stepping away. AOL Instant Messenger (1997) built a whole culture around being away: the "away message," often a song lyric or cryptic mood, was the Millennial teenager’s first public status update, and brb was its shortest form. It carried over into texting and online gaming ("brb, mom’s calling") and is still used, though Gen Z often just stops responding.
biblical_def: BRB is a small promise: I am stepping away, and I will return shortly. In chat and gaming it keeps the place warm; it tells the others not to give up on you. The Christian observation: the word is innocent, and it is also a little picture of one of the greatest promises ever made. The Lord Jesus, stepping away from His disciples, said: "And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again, and receive you unto myself; that where I am, there ye may be also" (Joh 14:3). The last promise in the Bible is the same: "Surely I come quickly" (Rev 22:20). His people live in the posture of those who were told "be right back," and the right response is watching: "Watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour wherein the Son of man cometh" (Mat 25:13). There is a second lesson in the small word. Our own promises to return are less certain than His. "Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth" (Pro 27:1), and James tells us to say, "If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that" (Jas 4:15). A father teaches his children to keep their small promises, including "I’ll be right back," because faithfulness in little is faithfulness; and to wait for the One whose "be right back" is the hope of the world.
webster_summary: Millennial chat initialism (1990s IRC / AIM) for be right back; a harmless small promise that pictures the great one: I will come again (Joh 14:3).
webster_full: BRB, interj. (Millennial chat, text, and gaming slang, 1990s–present; initialism of be right back) Announcing a brief absence. "brb, dinner." Related: AFK (away from keyboard), AIM "away message."

Webster (1828), root back: BACK, adverb To the place from which one came; as, to go back is to return. 2. In a figurative sense, to a former state, condition or station; as, he cannot go back from his engagements. 3. Behind; not advancing; not coming or bringing forward; as, to keep back a part; to keep one’s selfback. 4. Towards times or things past; as, to look back on former ages. 5. Again; in return; as, give back the money. 6. To go or come back is to return, either to a former place, or state. 7. To go or give back is to retreat to recede.
Decode for parents: "be right back" is a promise; teach your children to keep even the small ones.
scriptures: Joh 14:3
And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again, and receive you unto myself; that where I am, there ye may be also.
He which testifieth these things saith, Surely I come quickly. Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus.
Watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour wherein the Son of man cometh.
Pro 27:1
Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth.
Jas 4:15
For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that.
corruption_summary: BRB is harmless; its only shadow is the casual promise made without thought of God’s will, and its best use is as a reminder of Christ’s promise to come again.
corruption_paragraphs: If there is a corruption here, it is the presumption of the casual promise. We say "right back" as though our next hour were ours, and online culture has made the unkept promise normal: the "brb" that becomes three days of silence. Small broken promises teach a child that words are cheap. Scripture treats our tomorrows more soberly: they belong to God, and our plans are spoken under "If the Lord will." That is not superstition but honesty about who holds time.

The redemption is to let the little word point upward. Christ is the One who truly stepped away and truly promised to return, and the whole Church is a household keeping the lamps lit. "Surely I come quickly. Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus" (Rev 22:20). Teach the young to keep their word in small things, to hold their plans with open hands, and to live as servants whose Master has said He will be right back.
roots_summary: Old English baec (back) → be right back → 1990s IRC / AOL brb → AIM away-message culture → texting and gaming.
roots_lines: Old English baec — the back; on baec — backward, returning
1980s–90s: IRC and AOL chat initialism brb
1997–2000s: AIM away messages; AFK in gaming
2000s–present: texting and voice-chat shorthand
Biblical anchor: I will come again (Joh 14:3); surely I come quickly (Rev 22:20)
usage: "brb, grabbing a drink."
Christ’s "be right back": I will come again, and receive you unto myself (Joh 14:3).
Say it as James teaches: if the Lord will (Jas 4:15).

etymology: Initialism for talk to you later, a sign-off from 1990s chat rooms and AOL Instant Messenger that carried into 2000s texting. Lauren Myracle’s young-adult novel ttyl (2004), written entirely as instant messages between three high-school girls, made the initialism a generational emblem (and a frequently challenged library book). Variants: ttyl8r, ttys (talk to you soon), g2g (got to go).
biblical_def: TTYL is the instant-message goodbye: a friendly close that promises the conversation will pick up again. It belongs to the age when friendship moved onto screens, and a Millennial teenager might spend three hours a night in typed conversation with people he had seen all day at school. The Christian observation: the word is harmless, and the Bible itself contains the earliest version of it. The apostle John ended a letter this way: "Having many things to write unto you, I would not write with paper and ink: but I trust to come unto you, and speak face to face, that our joy may be full" (2Jn 1:12). John used the written word gladly, and he also knew it was second best. Some things wait for presence. That is the gentle correction for a generation that came to prefer the typed version of friendship. Scripture prizes godly conversation: "Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him" (Mal 3:16). It prizes the talk of the household, where the words of God are spoken "when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way" (Deu 6:7). A father teaches his children to use messages well, with speech "alway with grace, seasoned with salt" (Col 4:6), and to keep the best things for face to face.

corruption_summary: TTYL is harmless; its shadow is a generation that came to prefer typed friendship, and John’s own sign-off reminds us that joy is fullest face to face.
corruption_paragraphs: If there is drift here, it is the slow substitution of the message for the meeting. Instant messaging gave a generation constant contact and less presence: hours of conversation that could be paused, edited, and abandoned at will, and a habit of saying online what one would never say in person. Scripture does not despise letters; half the New Testament is mail. But the apostles kept pressing toward presence. "I trust I shall shortly see thee, and we shall speak face to face" (3Jn 1:14).

The recovery is ordered speech in both forms. Write well, because the Spirit inspired letters; speak well, because the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. A household that talks at its table, prays aloud together, and walks and speaks of the things of God by the way is practising the conversation that lasts. Let the young sign off with ttyl if they like, and then actually show up later.
